strengths: Comprehensive evaluation spanning synthetic (1M-token passkey retrieval), academic (SCROLLS, 2WikiMQA, HotpotQA), and real-world (user-behavior QA, terminal agent) tasks, giving reasonably convincing evidence of practical utility beyond narrow benchmarks.

The dual-memory design (gated global memory + FIFO temporary memory) is well-motivated and the ablations in Section 5.1 (varying memory allocation, removing the gate) provide clear evidence for the causal role of each component, which is a nontrivial and useful mechanistic analysis.

Strong length-extrapolation result: a model fine-tuned only on 32k contexts retrieves passkeys accurately across a 1M-token context, and efficiency curves (Figure 9) convincingly show linear time / constant memory versus full attention's quadratic/linear growth and OOM behavior.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy for training on long contexts is a genuinely useful systems contribution (2.7x speedup) that addresses a real bottleneck for this class of methods, going beyond pure modeling novelty.

Gating-value visualization (Figure 10, Appendix E) adds interpretability, showing plausible write/protect dynamics for a specific passkey example, which supports the mechanistic story rather than just aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: Key related methods explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., ARMT, HMT variants beyond HMT itself, Infini-attention) are not consistently included as experimental baselines, weakening the comparative claim of superiority over 'finite-state' memory methods generally rather than just the few tested.

Table 4's real-world results are difficult to interpret: Full Attention is reported only at 4k/32k for UQA and 128k for Terminal-Bench, while CoMeT is reported at 4k and 5k (memory budget, not context length is conflated with the Full-Attn context-length column), making direct comparison and the 'competitive with full attention' claim hard to verify without clearer methodology and matched conditions.

The paper's claim that CoMeT 'surpasses other efficient methods' holds on the SCROLLS average but not uniformly — e.g., LongLLMLingua and SWA beat CoMeT on QuALITY and ContractNLI — so the strength of the overall claim should be tempered and task-level variance discussed.

Extrapolation beyond training length (32k to 1M) is demonstrated only on the synthetic passkey task; there is no evidence that gains generalize to natural long-document understanding tasks beyond the 32k training regime, leaving the practical value of the million-token capability less substantiated for realistic use cases.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code is promised but not confirmed available at submission, real-world datasets (UQA, agent trajectories) are proprietary/anonymized and cannot be released, and some architectural hyperparameter choices (e.g., RLA rank r=8, compression token interleaving frequency) are asserted from 'preliminary experiments' without full ablation tables.

Evaluations appear to use a single base model (Qwen3-4B, with one Qwen3-8B agent experiment) and single runs without reported variance/significance testing, limiting confidence in the generality and robustness of the reported gains.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important problem (quadratic attention cost and unbounded KV-cache growth) with a reasonably clear architectural description (global gated memory + temporary FIFO memory + compression/readout tokens).

Efficiency analysis (prefill/decode latency, peak VRAM) convincingly demonstrates the claimed linear-time, constant-memory behavior relative to full attention, and is one of the more rigorous parts of the paper.
The layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy for training on long contexts is a useful, concrete engineering contribution with a reported 2.7x speedup over naive context parallelism.
Reasonably broad evaluation suite spanning SCROLLS, short-context QA, synthetic passkey retrieval to 1M tokens, and two real-world-motivated tasks (UQA, agent/Terminal-Bench).
Ablations (Section 5.1, Figure 7/8) and gate visualizations (Figure 10/11) offer some mechanistic insight into the respective roles of global vs. temporary memory.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the architecture largely recombines existing ideas (Transformer-XL-style chunk recurrence, Compressive-Transformer-style dual memory, RMT-style memory tokens, LSTM/GRU-style gating), and the paper's own related-work section cites ARMT as having a comparable associative/gated memory design, yet ARMT is never included as an experimental baseline -- a significant omission given it is the closest prior method.

The headline claim of handling 'arbitrarily long' contexts rests almost entirely on a single synthetic passkey-retrieval task; no finite-state or recurrent-Transformer baselines (HMT, Transformer-XL, ARMT, etc.) are evaluated at the same extreme lengths (up to 1M) to show CoMeT's advantage is not shared by competitors, making the extrapolation claim under-supported.

Real SCROLLS/QA evaluation lengths (≤~20k tokens) are far short of the advertised million-token capability, so there is no evidence the model preserves actual reasoning/comprehension quality (as opposed to a single-fact retrieval) at extreme lengths.

Reproducibility is undermined by the proprietary, non-public UQA dataset used for one of the two 'real-world' validations, and by the absence of released code/checkpoints at submission time; key training/evaluation details (e.g., exact memory settings used for the Terminal-Bench comparison, where 'CoMeT 5k' is compared against 'Full Attn 128k' without a matched-length baseline) are unclear or inconsistently presented (Table 4).
Baseline memory budgets are not uniformly controlled (e.g., SWA/Transformer-XL window of 5120 vs. ~3k for others), which could bias the SCROLLS comparison in CoMeT's favor.

Results are reported as single runs without variance/significance information, and some comparisons (e.g., CoMeT's custom 2560-token budget vs. baselines' 3072-token nominal budget) make head-to-head efficiency-controlled comparison difficult to verify precisely.

strengths: Well-motivated dual-memory architecture combining a gated global memory for long-range retention with a FIFO temporary memory for fine-grained recent context, directly targeting known weaknesses of prior finite-state/recurrent Transformers (lack of gating, loss of recent detail).

Strong and diverse empirical evidence: near-perfect passkey retrieval extrapolation from 32k training to 1M-token contexts, competitive/near-parity results with a fine-tuned full-attention baseline on SCROLLS summarization tasks, and consistent matching of full attention on short-context QA (2WikiMQA/HotpotQA), suggesting no regression on in-distribution short inputs.

Concrete, well-measured efficiency gains (constant ~10GB memory vs. OOM for full attention at 128k+, linear prefill vs. quadratic, stable ~22ms/token decode vs. linearly growing full-attention latency), backed by actual wall-clock/VRAM curves rather than only asymptotic claims.

Useful ablations isolating the distinct roles of global vs. temporary memory (Figure 7/8) and demonstrating the necessity of the gating mechanism via a clean failure-mode experiment (no-gate collapse), plus a gate-value visualization offering some mechanistic insight.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism for training is a genuine engineering contribution with a measured 2.7x speedup, addressing a real practical bottleneck for fine-tuning memory-augmented models on very long sequences.
Evaluation spans synthetic, academic (SCROLLS), and real-world (UQA, agent/Terminal-Bench) settings, strengthening the case for practical relevance beyond narrow benchmark performance.
weaknesses: A highly relevant prior architecture, Infini-attention (Munkhdalai et al. 2024), which also combines local attention with a compressive/gated memory for infinite context and is even used as the source of the passkey task, is never discussed in related work nor included as an experimental baseline; this is a significant gap given the conceptual similarity and undermines the novelty and completeness-of-comparison claims.

The claim that CoMeT 'outperforms other efficient methods' on SCROLLS is only true on average; per-task results are mixed (e.g., QuALITY F1 56.0 is well below LongLLMLingua 65.9 and EXIT 59.9; NarrativeQA 22.6 is close to but not above ActivationBeacon 23.2), so the headline comparison somewhat overstates uniform superiority.

No code is currently released (placeholder link only) and one of the real-world evaluation datasets (UQA) is proprietary/anonymized, limiting independent verification and reproducibility of the practical-application claims.

All main experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B, with one agent experiment on Qwen3-8B); there is no evidence the architecture and gains generalize across model families or larger scales, which matters for claims about broad applicability to LLMs.

Results appear to be single-run without variance/error bars or significance testing across the many benchmark comparisons, making it hard to assess whether reported gaps (e.g., CoMeT vs. SWA/HMT on SCROLLS) are robust rather than run-to-run noise.

Training CoMeT at 128k context requires 16x80GB GPUs, a substantial compute barrier that limits accessibility and independent reproduction of the long-context training pipeline, despite the paper's efficiency-focused framing.

The RLA module's added parameter/compute overhead and its interaction with model quality are not quantified in detail, leaving some ambiguity about the actual 'minimal fine-tuning' and parameter-efficiency claims.

strengths: The dual-memory design (gated global memory for long-range retention + FIFO temporary memory for fine-grained recency) is well-motivated and the paper provides a clear mechanistic decomposition of what each component contributes, backed by targeted ablations (Fig. 7, Fig. 8) that isolate the role of global vs. temporary memory and the gating mechanism.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: SCROLLS benchmark across 7 tasks, extrapolation beyond training length, 1M-token passkey retrieval from 32k training, real-world user-behavior QA and agent/coding tasks (Terminal-Bench), and generalization across three model families/scales (Qwen3-4B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B).

Thorough efficiency characterization (prefill/decode latency and memory vs. full attention, and additional comparison to RWKV7), supporting the constant-memory/linear-time claims with concrete measurements rather than only asymptotic argument.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism for training on very long contexts is a useful systems contribution with a demonstrated 2.7× speedup over naive context parallelism, enabling 128k-context fine-tuning on modest GPU budgets.

Interpretability analysis (gating value visualization across layers) provides some mechanistic evidence that the gate behaves as intended (closing after storing salient facts), which strengthens the causal story behind the architecture rather than relying purely on aggregate metrics.

Transparent limitations and failure-case analysis (Appendix J) showing that CoMeT's failure modes are largely shared with full attention rather than unique artifacts of compression, which adds credibility to the evaluation.
weaknesses: Missing direct empirical comparison against the closest prior finite-state memory architectures explicitly discussed as motivation (ARMT, RMT, Compressive Transformer); only Transformer-XL, SWA, and HMT are benchmarked, leaving the paper's central novelty claim (addressing gaps in prior finite-state models) only partially substantiated experimentally.

The UQA real-world evaluation relies on a proprietary, anonymized e-commerce dataset that cannot be released, limiting reproducibility of one of the three main experimental pillars; the code repository link in the abstract is also a placeholder with no URL provided.

The extrapolation results on genuinely long realistic documents (Appendix D, SCROLLS subset >32k) show CoMeT still lags noticeably behind full attention (e.g., 38.6 vs 48.8 ROUGE-1 on GovRep), which tempers the headline claim of essentially unlimited high-fidelity extrapolation suggested by the passkey results; the passkey task itself is a narrow synthetic probe that may not represent general long-context reasoning at extreme lengths.

Results are reported as single-run numbers without variance/seed information or statistical testing, making it hard to assess whether small margins over baselines (e.g., CoMeT vs. SWA in some SCROLLS subtasks) are robust.

Given the crowded space of recurrent/memory-augmented Transformer variants (Compressive Transformer, RMT, ARMT, HMT, Memformer), the specific architectural novelty (RLA module, gated FIFO+global memory) is somewhat incremental engineering rather than a conceptually new mechanism, and the ablations, while informative, do not fully disentangle which specific design choice (vs. simply more careful tuning/larger effective memory budget) drives the gains over HMT/SWA.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem (quadratic cost / unbounded KV cache in long-context LLMs) with a reasonably well-motivated architectural combination of gated global memory and FIFO temporary memory.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism for training on very long contexts is a genuine systems contribution, with a demonstrated 2.7x throughput improvement over naive context parallelism, enabling 128k-token fine-tuning on modest hardware.

Broad empirical coverage: SCROLLS benchmark, shorter-context QA, 1M-token passkey extrapolation, efficiency profiling (latency/memory), and generalization tests across three model families/scales (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B).
Reasonably thorough ablations dissecting the distinct roles of global vs. temporary memory (Figs. 7-8), gate necessity, RLA rank sensitivity, and chunk-size/compression-interval choices.
Includes an honest qualitative failure-case analysis (Appendix J) showing CoMeT's errors are not categorically worse than full attention's, which is a commendable transparency practice.
weaknesses: Critical missing baselines undermine the central comparative claims: ARMT (Associative Recurrent Memory Transformer) is repeatedly cited in the introduction and related work as the closest prior method lacking explicit gating—exactly the gap CoMeT claims to fill—yet it is never empirically compared against in Table 2 or elsewhere. Infini-Attention (Munkhdalai et al. 2024), the source of the passkey task and an architecturally similar gated compressive-memory method, is also never used as a baseline despite being highly relevant.

Novelty is incremental: the components (gated additive state update reminiscent of LSTM/GRU gates, FIFO recent-token cache akin to Transformer-XL/sliding-window caching, readout/compression tokens akin to gist tokens) are individually well-established; the main contribution is their combination plus a low-rank adapter, which is a relatively modest conceptual advance given the related-work framing suggests a larger gap being closed.

Reproducibility concerns: the 'real-world' UQA benchmark is drawn from a proprietary, anonymized e-commerce dataset, and the agent/Terminal-Bench evaluation relies on an internally curated, non-public trajectory dataset generated by an undisclosed 'expert' agent model. Neither can be independently verified or reproduced, weakening the evidentiary value of the practical-utility claims.

No statistical rigor anywhere in the paper: all reported numbers (SCROLLS scores, UQA/Terminal-Bench results, ablations) appear to be single runs with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, making it difficult to assess whether reported gains (e.g., CoMeT vs. SWA differences of 1-2 points) are meaningful.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: CoMeT underperforms several baselines on individual SCROLLS subtasks (e.g., Qspr, QALT, CNLI) and underperforms full attention on Terminal-Bench (20.27 vs 21.33), tempering the 'comparable to full attention' framing used in the abstract.

The headline passkey result (1M-token retrieval after training only on the passkey task at 32k) is a narrow single-fact synthetic benchmark that memory-augmented architectures are known to solve well when explicitly optimized for it; it provides limited evidence of general long-range reasoning capability, and the heatmap figures (1a, 8) lack precise quantitative accuracy numbers.

The 'accessible, practical, plug-in' framing in the abstract/conclusion is in tension with the substantial infrastructure (16×80GB GPUs with custom pipeline parallelism) required to actually fine-tune the module at the context lengths used in key experiments.

strengths: Well-motivated dual-memory architecture (gated global memory + FIFO temporary memory) that cleanly addresses two failure modes of prior finite-state recurrent Transformers: catastrophic forgetting of long-range info and loss of fine-grained recent detail.

Strong empirical breadth: SCROLLS benchmark results show CoMeT outperforms a wide range of efficient baselines (compression-based and finite-state) and nearly matches fine-tuned full attention on summarization with only ~2.5k memory tokens.

Impressive length extrapolation: a model fine-tuned only on 32k contexts retrieves a passkey correctly across a 1M-token context, with clear linear-time/constant-memory efficiency curves (Fig. 1, Fig. 9) backed by concrete latency/VRAM measurements.

Useful systems contribution: the layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy for training on very long contexts (2.7x speedup over naive context parallelism) is a practical enabler and is reasonably well described with bubble visualizations.

Reasonably thorough ablations (memory allocation roles, RLA rank sensitivity, chunk size/compression stride) and generalization checks across three model families/scales (Qwen3-4B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B), which support the robustness of the core claims.

The paper includes an honest failure-case analysis (Appendix J) showing that CoMeT's errors are qualitatively similar to full-attention failures in several cases, which strengthens credibility over cherry-picked positive results.
Real-world evaluations (user behavior QA, Terminal-Bench agent tasks) add practical relevance beyond synthetic/academic benchmarks.
weaknesses: The core architectural ideas (chunked gated memory update reminiscent of LSTM/GRU gating, FIFO temporary memory, readout/compression tokens) are largely a recombination of existing techniques from Transformer-XL, RMT, HMT, and Compressive Transformer; the novelty is incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Memory budget comparability across baselines is only approximate (CoMeT's default 512G+2048T=2560 vs. baselines' ~3072), which slightly complicates head-to-head fairness claims despite being described as controlled.

The passkey retrieval task, while a compelling extrapolation demonstration, is a relatively easy single-needle retrieval task; it does not stress multi-fact aggregation or complex reasoning over extremely long contexts (as acknowledged implicitly by the Qasper aggregation failure case).

On the agent/code task (Terminal-Bench), CoMeT slightly underperforms full attention (20.27 vs 21.33) and is only tested at one context length/model size, limiting the strength of the 'practical validation' claim in that setting.
The UQA real-world benchmark relies on a proprietary, non-public e-commerce dataset and LLM-as-judge evaluation, which limits reproducibility and independent verification of that result.

No reported variance across seeds or statistical significance testing for the main benchmark comparisons, despite fairly small numeric gaps between CoMeT and some baselines (e.g., SWA, HMT) on individual SCROLLS subtasks.

The framing of 'arbitrarily long sequences' with 'constant memory' somewhat overstates the practical capacity limits of a fixed-size memory state, as the failure-case analysis itself shows information loss and aggregation failures even within moderate-length documents (Qasper).
The code repository link is left blank in the submitted manuscript, which is a reproducibility concern at review time even though code is promised.
